title: Television grew out of radio's networks
description: American TV borrowed radio's networks: NBC's 1926 radio chain, its Blue network that became ABC, and NBC's own TV network by 1948.

facts.text: Television was first regarded by many as 'radio with pictures.'
In 1948 television was still in its experimental stage, and radio remained the number one broadcast medium.
NBC was formed in 1926; on November 15, 1926, 25 radio stations in 21 cities carried its first network program from New York.
After the FCC refused licenses to companies running more than one network, NBC was forced to sell its Blue radio network, which became ABC.
NBC began operating its first television station in 1939, and by 1948 its TV network had 47 stations.

title: Radio's stars and sponsors came to TV
description: Radio stars hesitated, then followed Milton Berle into TV; CBS lured NBC's radio stars in 1948; and advertising, radio's way of paying, became TV's too.

facts.text: Most of radio's biggest stars, such as Jack Benny, Bob Hope, and George Burns and Gracie Allen, were at first reluctant to risk their careers on television.

Milton Berle, who had had little success on radio, starred in NBC's Texaco Star Theatre from 1948; it was TV's first hit and led to a dramatic increase in TV set sales, earning him the name Mr. Television.
When Texaco Star Theatre debuted in 1948, fewer than 2 percent of US homes had a TV set; by 1956, TV was in 70 percent of homes.
In 1948 CBS chief William S. Paley signed radio stars away from NBC, including Jack Benny, George Burns and Gracie Allen, and Amos 'n' Andy's creators; they proved as popular on TV as on radio.
CBS began as a radio network in the late 1920s and grew under William S. Paley.
Advertising became the principal means of support for broadcasting in the United States; sponsored network programs furnished revenue to both the network and its stations.
On NBC radio, breakout hits on the Blue network were often moved to the more popular Red network at the request of sponsors.

title: Three networks ruled prime time
description: Four networks started regular schedules in 1948; DuMont folded, and ABC, CBS and NBC held more than 90 percent of the prime-time audience in the late 1970s.

facts.text: Regular programming on the four networks, ABC, CBS, NBC and DuMont, was scarce until the fall of 1948; DuMont folded in the mid-1950s.
Prime time is the evening block from 8 to 11 PM Eastern time.
In the late 1970s, more than 90 percent of the US prime-time viewing audience watched ABC, CBS or NBC.

title: The network era's shared screen
description: With nearly every home tuned to the same three networks, TV became cultural glue: a big event like the 1960 debate reached most of the country at once.

facts.text: By 1960 nearly 90 percent of American homes had a television.
On September 26, 1960, the first televised presidential debate, between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon, was simulcast on all three networks and reached a then-record audience of about 70 million.
Britannica calls radio and television a kind of cultural glue: from 1929 to 1989, nearly the entire country, young and old, rich and poor, fed from the same cultural trough.
Control of television by three companies produced a unified mass culture whose products were experienced by nearly everyone.

title: Live TV drama and the anthology series
description: Early network TV was mostly live; anthology series staged a new play each week, and writers such as Paddy Chayefsky and Rod Serling made their names.

facts.text: In the early 1950s most network television was broadcast live; by the early 1960s most was recorded.
Most TV plays of the era were anthology dramas, weekly series presenting original and adapted plays under one title, such as Kraft Television Theatre (1947 to 1958) and Studio One (1948 to 1958).
Young writers such as Paddy Chayefsky, Rod Serling and Gore Vidal wrote highly regarded teleplays for the network anthology series.
Marty began as a 1953 television play and became a 1955 film that won the Academy Award for best picture.

title: From kinescope to videotape
description: Before 1956, TV could be recorded only by filming a monitor (a kinescope), which was costly and poor; Ampex's videotape, and filmed Hollywood series, ended the live era.

facts.text: Before videotape, the only way to record TV was on film: a movie camera pointed at a TV monitor made a kinescope, which was developed and later projected for broadcast in other time zones.
Kinescope recordings were poor in quality and expensive, since the film could be used only once; by 1954 TV broadcasters were using more raw film than the entire movie industry.
In 1956 Ampex introduced the first practical videotape recorder for TV stations and networks, replacing kinescope film.
On November 30, 1956, CBS taped a live New York newscast on an Ampex recorder in Hollywood and rebroadcast it hours later to the West Coast.
TV production moved to the Los Angeles area, the live theatrical style gave way to shows recorded on film, and filmed shows could earn income indefinitely from reruns.

title: What a sitcom is
description: A situation comedy is a half-hour series with a continuing cast in the same setting, week after week; I Love Lucy grew from a radio comedy.

facts.text: The sitcom was a 30-minute format featuring a continuing cast of characters that appeared in the same setting week after week.
I Love Lucy (CBS, 1951 to 1957), starring Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, debuted in October 1951; it was shot on film in Hollywood rather than broadcast live from New York.
I Love Lucy was adapted for TV from My Favorite Husband, a CBS radio comedy in which Lucille Ball starred from 1948.
I Love Lucy's early episodes took place mostly in a New York apartment building, where Lucy and Ricky Ricardo lived near their landlords and friends, Fred and Ethel Mertz.

title: I Love Lucy's three-camera method
description: Filmed on 35 mm with three cameras before a live audience and edited on a four-headed Moviola, I Love Lucy set the sitcom standard and could be rerun.

facts.text: Most TV shows were then made in the East, broadcast live there and shown to western time zones as kinescope copies, which a Library of Congress specialist likened to watching TV through a cheesecloth; Ball and Arnaz chose to produce their show in Hollywood.

Cinematographer Karl Freund and director Marc Daniels are generally credited with filming I Love Lucy with three cameras in front of a live audience, the technique that became the standard for sitcoms.
I Love Lucy was shot on 35 mm film before a live audience, with one lighting system for the whole set.

With three motion picture cameras, I Love Lucy could be filmed continuously and in sequence, like a stage play; editor Dann Cahn cut it on a Moviola with four heads, three for picture and one for sound.
Because it was produced on film, I Love Lucy could be shown again, and in 1955 it became one of the first series broadcast as reruns.

title: The evening news grows to half an hour
description: Network evening newscasts ran 15 minutes until 1963, when CBS under Walter Cronkite, and then the others, expanded to half an hour.

facts.text: In 1963 the network evening news programs expanded from 15 minutes to half an hour.
Walter Cronkite became anchor of the CBS evening news in 1962; soon after, its 15 minutes became 30, the first half-hour nightly news show on American network television.

title: Vietnam, the first television war
description: Vietnam was the first televised war: evening news showed film, flown in by air, of planes and patrols, and in 1968 Cronkite went to see for himself.

facts.text: The Vietnam War was the first war to be televised; Americans regularly saw film of airplanes flying, often dropping bombs, and troops on patrol, sometimes in combat.
Film of the Vietnam War usually reached the networks as cans of film shipped by air, arriving a few days later.
In 1968 Walter Cronkite left the anchor desk to report from Vietnam after the Tet Offensive and declared that the war could end only in a stalemate.

title: From single sponsors to commercials
description: After the rigged quiz shows of the late 1950s, networks took shows away from single sponsors and sold short commercial slots, like ad pages in a magazine.

facts.text: In 1958 former contestants revealed that big-money TV quiz shows were rigged and contestants coached; a House subcommittee held hearings in 1959.
After the quiz show scandals, networks grew wary of single-sponsor programs and sold advertising time in 15-, 30- and 60-second units, taking control from sponsors and ad agencies.

Producers took full control of shows and stations sold commercial time, following the model of magazines and newspapers; removing advertisers from the shows removed their urge to interfere with content.

title: Nielsen ratings price the audience
description: From 1950 Nielsen measured viewing in a sample of homes with Audimeters and diaries; ratings and shares set what advertising on each program costs.

facts.text: From 1950 A.C. Nielsen rated TV shows using a sample of more than 1,000 TV homes; each had a small box, the Audimeter, attached to the set to record when it was on and what channel it was tuned to, and a smaller group kept viewing diaries.
A Nielsen rating of 20 means 20 percent of all US TV households tuned in to a program; a 30 share means 30 percent of the people watching TV at that time watched it.
Commercial networks use ratings, in part, to set advertising rates for each program and to decide which programs to continue or cancel.

title: The Public Broadcasting Act of 1967
description: Calls for less commercial TV led to the 1967 Act, proposed by the Carnegie Commission, which created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and led to PBS and NPR.

facts.text: After the quiz show hearings, columnists such as Walter Lippmann called for a new kind of television modeled on the BBC, calls that led toward a publicly funded system.
On November 7, 1967, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Public Broadcasting Act, which created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.
The Public Broadcasting Act was proposed by the Carnegie Commission on educational television.
Johnson said the Corporation for Public Broadcasting would get part of its support from the government but be carefully guarded from government or party control.
The Public Broadcasting Act led to the establishment of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, PBS and NPR.

title: Sesame Street teaches with TV's own tricks
description: The Children's Television Workshop built Sesame Street (1969) with educators and researchers to prepare low-income children for school, borrowing commercial TV's pace and repetition.

facts.text: The first episode of Sesame Street, sponsored by the letters W, S and E and the numbers 2 and 3, aired in the fall of 1969.
Joan Ganz Cooney, a New York public TV producer, founded the Children's Television Workshop in 1968 with backing from the Carnegie and Ford Foundations and the US Commissioner of Education.
Sesame Street was designed by education professionals and child psychologists to help low-income and minority children aged 2 to 5 arrive at school better prepared.
Cooney consulted dozens of educators and set up a collaboration with educators and child development researchers to plan the show.
Sesame Street debuted in 1969 on National Educational Television, which became PBS in 1970, and features animations, live actors and Jim Henson's Muppets.
Cooney based Sesame Street's fast pace, repeated segments and mix of formats on 1960s commercial television.
Signing the Public Broadcasting Act, Johnson said the new corporation would try to prove that what educates can also be exciting.

title: Cable's start, HBO and CNN
description: Cable began in the late 1940s to fix poor reception; HBO (1972) sold commercial-free films and went national by satellite in 1975; CNN (1980) brought 24-hour news.

facts.text: US cable-television systems began in the late 1940s to improve reception of network broadcasts in remote and hilly areas.
Some cable systems can deliver 50 or more channels.
HBO started in 1972 showing uncut, commercial-free movies, and cable subscribers paid extra for it.
In 1975 HBO became the first American network to deliver its programming by satellite, and thus the first national cable channel.
CNN began in 1980 and ushered in the era of 24-hour television news.

title: Cable splits the audience
description: As cable reached most homes, the three networks' share fell, and channels aimed at special interests divided viewers, ending the shared network era.

facts.text: Only 8 percent of US households had basic cable in 1970, 23 percent in 1980, and nearly 60 percent by the end of the 1980s.
By 1989 the three networks' share of the prime-time audience was down to 67 percent.
In the 1990s cable services aimed at specific audiences with specialized interests grew fastest, dividing the audience into smaller and smaller segments.
Britannica says the era of a unified mass culture shaped by three networks ended, in effect, in the 1990s, when audiences stopped watching the same things at the same time.

title: Streaming puts viewers in charge
description: Netflix went from DVDs by mail (1997) to streaming (2007) to whole seasons at once (2013), letting viewers watch at their own pace on any screen.

facts.text: Netflix was founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph as a DVD-rental service; subscribers ordered online and received discs by mail.
In 2007 Netflix introduced streaming, letting subscribers watch directly over the Internet.
In February 2013 Netflix made all 13 first-season episodes of House of Cards available at once, instead of one episode a week.
Viewers quickly embraced having all episodes of a new season to watch at their own pace, on whatever screen they wish.

title: Binge viewing changes how series are written
description: Binge-watching (many episodes in a row) is older than streaming, but autoplay made it effortless, and writers began shaping seasons as one long story.

facts.text: To binge-watch is to watch many or all episodes of a TV series in rapid succession.
Binge viewing predates Netflix: cable networks aired marathons of classic shows in the late 1990s, and binging became routine with TV on DVD a decade later.
On Netflix, the next episode of a series queues up automatically as soon as the previous one ends.
Broadcast TV writers build peril at the end of each act to keep viewers watching through commercial breaks.
Writer Marc Bernardin notes that binge viewers skip the 'previously on' recap and that writers describe a streaming season as 'breaking a 10-hour movie'.

title: Newton Minow's 'vast wasteland'
description: In 1961 FCC chairman Newton Minow called commercial TV a vast wasteland, pushed the networks toward longer news and won the first federal money for educational TV.

facts.text: In May 1961, FCC chairman Newton Minow, appointed by President Kennedy, told the National Association of Broadcasters that commercial television was a 'vast wasteland' and argued for public service television.
Minow encouraged the commercial networks to expand their nightly news from 15 minutes to half an hour.
Minow pushed through the Educational Television Facilities Act of 1962, the first federal funds for educational TV, a step that led five years later to the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967.
